item.title: Hello, is this a robot? Why voice systems in telephony might be better than they seem at first glance
item.description:
Attitudes towards AI in customer support are, to put it mildly, mixed. Companies are actively using voice assistants, even though customers are often not thrilled with such 'helpers.' Let's discuss why you should give a chance to the robot on the other end of the line and in which tasks AI voice systems can excel, including thanks to new frameworks for developing intelligent telephony systems. We also share a selection of open-source tools for creating multimodal voice agents. Read more

item.title: Identify me if you can! How deepfakes are changing IT hiring (and not only)
item.description:
Interviews are increasingly becoming a vector for cyberattacks. Attackers use deepfakes to impersonate real candidates and recruiters, or spread malware disguised as test assignments – sending "harmless" code or a dependency package that, when run on the victim's device, installs malicious software. Today, we at Beeline Cloud decided to discuss the methods used by fake applicants and recruiters, how to recognize an attacker "on the other side of the resume," and what AI has to do with it. Read more

item.title: How I Create AI Memory from Telegram Chats: Tens of Thousands of Messages, Thousands of Facts, Hundreds of People
item.description:
At night, around 2 AM Moscow time, the server wakes up and starts a pipeline. First, the service goes to Telegram and downloads new messages from chats that the user has marked. An hour later, a second worker starts and turns these messages into memory: it chunks them, processes them through DeepSeek, organizes them into tables, and exports them to markdown files. By morning, the user has additional information in the second memory service. The second memory service is not just a chat history. Six months later, you can ask, 'What budget did we agree on for the trip then?' and get an answer with a link to a specific message in a specific chat. Strangely enough, almost all my work on creating the service was not in working with LLMs. So what was it?

item.title: Copilot went online for an answer. You won't see it in Word, but an administrator in Purview will.
item.description:
Web search in Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Chat is available to users unless an administrator disables it with one of two policies. No separate "allow assistant internet access" setting is required. The assistant generates its own search query, which is visible in three different places: in Copilot Chat, citations are available for 24 hours; in the assistant pane within Microsoft 365 apps (like Word or PowerPoint), they are not visible at all; and administrators can view the same search terms alongside the prompt and response via the activity explorer in Purview DSPM for AI. The analysis is based on two learn.microsoft.com pages: citations from the web search page were verified on September 6, 2026, and the second page was re-verified on the same day. Inside, there are two diagrams and a table of "prompt - generated query" examples that you can replicate on your own tenant. Who sees this query and for how long.

item.title: Three models with 95% accuracy. Why can their chain only give 85%?
item.description:
For example, one participant chooses the cat branch, another the dog. The system can save both branches, request a higher quality image, or pass it to a human. To do this, the architecture needs pre-existing access to the source object, the ability to revise the route, and a limit on the number of additional attempts. If there is no such possibility, the detected disagreement will remain a beautiful entry in the log. Agreement also does not guarantee anything. All participants can confidently repeat the same mistake. Therefore, it is necessary to check a specific question: does disagreement help to identify errors better than a cheaper signal from one model, with a comparable budget? Works on deep ensembles provide grounds for exploring ensembles as a way to assess uncertainty. But in them, useful diversity arises even when training networks of the same architecture. Separately, the authors of Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents show that combining the answers of different LLMs does not always win against combining several answers from one strong model. Read more

item.title: Why Vector Databases Are Needed in the Era of LLMs
item.description:
Keyword search is no longer sufficient. To enable neural networks to provide accurate answers based on your corporate knowledge bases, they need to 'understand' the meaning of text, which is more complex than simple exact matches. This article explores how vector databases work, why they are essential for modern RAG, how they differ from traditional relational databases, and how to choose the right tool for your project.

item.title: Not Touching Model Weights: How We Built Alice AI's Research Agent and Drastically Reduced GPU Consumption
item.description:
My name is Prokhor, and I lead the 'Explore' agent team – a deep research mode in Alice AI chat. Deep Research is a special mode that creates a unique plan to solve user tasks, performs hundreds of searches, can visit websites (even with dynamic JavaScript), write and execute Python code, work with downloaded files, and more. All this is to provide the best answer to complex queries like 'Plan a two-week trip to Dagestan by car with children.' Over a year, the agent evolved from its first prototype to production, improving response quality, speed, and GPU consumption. Ruslan Iliev, the product manager, was responsible for the product side, defining goals, tools, and validation sets, and overseeing the launch. I'll explain how we got here – through a discarded prototype, dozens of wrapper layers, and a couple of painful lessons. Welcome!

item.title: MCP, so that the neural network can recommend movies without guessing
item.description:
I've always wanted conversations with a neural network about movies to go beyond just titles in a chat or suggestions to buy tickets yourself. It's a strange outcome: a person asks an assistant to do the work for them, and the assistant, in response, gives them, for example, a guess about where to buy tickets for that movie, instead of a precise result. In my movie service, I've created MCP. It can be connected to an AI agent as an external data source: MCP gives the neural network not just general internet search, but actual actions within a specific user's movie database, as well as a general movie database. For example, the agent can look at movies the user hasn't watched yet (for movies to watch in the future, there's a "Unwatched" section), use past ratings to find a movie the user would be interested in, compile a selection, find a link to buy tickets for a specific movie, and much more. The service is absolutely free! In this article, I'd like to talk about possible scenarios and the ones I use myself. I'll show it using Grok as an example, but it can be connected to any AI agent like Claude, Codex, Cursor, etc. If there are any movie lovers here, I'd be happy to receive feedback on MCP! Read about neural networks and movies
